newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's reformist president faces tests ahead of re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's reformist president faces tests ahead of re-election.

text.p: After pulling off the biggest coup of his administration, Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso still faces a series of obstacles before he seeks an unprecedented second term of office.

Cardoso was characteristically low-key after seeing Brazil's Senate give final approval Wednesday to legislation allowing him to become the first president in Brazil's history to run for a consecutive term of office. Cardoso made no public statement Thursday, and said through a spokesman Wednesday he was "satisfied."

But he had much to celebrate. Besides the change to the constitution allowing him to run again, international investors rewarded Cardoso's economic reform drive by bidding in droves on $3 billion worth of 30-year global bonds Wednesday, legitimising Brazil's creditworthiness after its 1980s debt crisis.
In addition, Brazil auctioned a concession for cellular telephone service around the capital city of Brasilia, a first step toward breaking up the state telecommunications monopoly.
"Three victories for the government," chimed a front-page headline in Jornal do Brasil.

Beyond Wednesday's sweep of successes, the 65-year-old former sociology professor is guaranteed a place in Brazilian history books as the author of the "Plano Real," a plan that anchored Brazil's real currency to the dollar in 1994, crushing annualized inflation of 5,000 percent in 1994 to a mere 10 percent in 1996.

But Cardoso still has his work cut out for him. Two key pieces of legislation, on civil service and pension reform, are virtually stalled in Congress. And the lack of those tools has kept Cardoso from attacking Brazil's most intractable economic problem, its gaping current account deficit -- around $27 billion at last count.
"The difficulties are not going to stop overnight," said political consultant Murillo Aragao. "Just because re-election has been approved, it doesn't mean everything is perfect."

Cardoso recently had seen a dismal few months marked by fighting among government allies, an alleged corruption scandal, a high-profile demonstration by the radical Landless Movement, and a slump in his popularity.

Democracy in Brazil is still a recent and somewhat disjointed affair, marked by shifting party loyalties, rocked by regular allegations of corruption and tolerated by a deeply cynical public. Its next elections are coming in October 1998.

A military government ruled until 1985. Brazil's first freely elected president Fernando Collor de Mello came from the back-country state of Alagoas. A telegenic scion of the Brazilian Globo media empire, Collor was drummed out of office in 1992 amid a corruption scandal.
He was succeeded by his vice president, Itamar Franco, a reluctant chief of state more comfortable in the company of glamorous models.
It was Franco who named then-Senator Cardoso to Finance Minister, and in that position he developed the economic plan that eventually catapulted him to the presidency.
In the most recent opinion polls, Cardoso's approval rating was down to 50 percent in May, a slump from a high of 70 percent in March. At present there is no strong challenger in sight.

Political consultant Paulo Kramer noted the final approval of the re-election bill marked the beginning of the 1998 election campaign which, for the time being, has only one serious candidate: Cardoso.

"But don't forget that a year and a half before the last election, no one imagined Fernando Henrique would be president and Fernando Collor (who won the 1989 presidential election) was a surprise too," Kramer said.
